utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. May we hear first the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Nicholas Koumjian, Ann Sutherland, and Ruth Karper for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. John Ostojic and Branko Lukic and Danilo Cirkovic on behalf of Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we start today, after having had a long break, let us hear, what are the witnesses to be expected for this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, for this week, the Defence will be calling Witness Number 70. And I'm informed, Your Honour, that there was a holiday in the former Yugoslavia on Thursday and Friday, and when the Court communicated with the Defence to request further witnesses, that it was impossible for us to obtain transportation and/or the necessary authorisations for them to be brought here. In addition, if I may, with all due respect, Your Honour, the Defence was under the misguided impression that two witnesses that the Court was going to call would appear no later than Friday, February 24th. So we anticipated in our scheduling that those witnesses would be called early this week, specifically starting perhaps as early as Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This, you are anticipating what I wanted to ask the Defence. The Defence knew that we would have an entire week sitting the entire day. And no doubt, it needs some justification for not calling witnesses save one witness, we learned from the provisional proffer, that will at least take us approximately two hours. Two hours of examination-in-chief for one week, this, no doubt, is not sufficient. And having reviewed the transcript, I can't find any basis for the Defence to believe that there would be witnesses available, in this case, Chamber witnesses. From the outset, it was the Defence telling this Trial Chamber that these two envisaged witnesses were not prepared to appear as witnesses for the Defence. No doubt, we called them, and we called them with a deadline. But there was no confirmation at all, not the slightest hint, that these witnesses would come during this week. So therefore, there is no sound basis for this. And there's no sound basis to believe that these Chamber witnesses would come. In fact, in this moment, we don't know what will happen, whether we have to subpoena them, whether they will arrive subpoenaed or not. As you know, this is not in our hands. But it's in your hand and it's your obligation to call witnesses that we can hear the entire week. And therefore, we are a little bit late because we had some deliberations beforehand. The question is: If so, if there is no justification for your proceeding, if it's necessary from the side of the Bench to take sanctions against the Defence, sanctions that would range from a stern warning up to the request to the Registrar to deduct parts of the fees of Defence counsel for frivolous actions as seen by the Appeals Chamber in cases in the past as an inherent power of the Chamber. So I would invite you to give furthermore justification for not calling additional witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure, Your Honour, if we can satisfy the Court's request for further justification. However, we would like to reply if we may in connection with the scenario that has presented itself here this week. Unbeknownst to the Defence, we did not anticipate this problem to occur. We contact the Victim and Witness Protection Unit to coordinate and to get the witnesses there, based both on their schedule as well as the immigration rules that are applicable. We are unable to at this time to have any other witnesses other than Witness Number 70 as previously stated. However, if permitted, I'd like to put in context and address some of the Court's concerns. Witnesses we believe for all sides are very difficult to ascertain and to bring on short notice. It is based on information and belief, although we hesitate to comment on this, the week prior to last, the OTP in the Brdjanin case also had a similar problem where they had to suspend a day, if not two, because of unavailability of witnesses. We agree and acknowledge our obligations to present the witnesses. We continue to assert and state for the Court that this will not interfere with the previously agreed-upon deadline of the Defence case of March 21st, 2003. It's something that we did not envision. It was not something that is intentionally before us today. We ask and appeal the Court not to enter sanctions. I think if the Court reviews respectfully the schedule and the pace of the proceedings, the Defence has been diligent in presenting the evidence that it wishes to bring forth. We likewise have streamlined some of the witnesses and our Defence case. We have converted some witnesses to Rule 92 bis witnesses. We also, as we reported in the previously scheduled 65 ter conference, that our list is getting pared down, and we expect and are thankful for the week that we had to prepare with our experts, and will provide the Court and the OTP with their reports on the deadline that the Court imposed of March 3rd, 2003. We have also, based on the Court's order, scheduled for the experts to proceed in the last ten days of the schedule, namely, commenced on or about March 12th and concluding on or about March 21st for our two experts. Prior to that time, we expect to call the remaining eight to ten witnesses that the Defence has, and we think we can conclude our case in ample time. Again, we would only like to cite to the Court and reconfirm that this is not an intentional attempt on our part to frustrate the process. It is something that has come up on short notice and the unavailability of our witnesses due to matters that we raised even as recent as ten days ago in private session with the Court. Quite candidly, that issue continues to raise its head, and witnesses are reluctant to even discuss things with us, much less to appear in light of the discussions that we had with the Court in private session. Mind you, the Defence would like to reiterate their request to have the OTP cease and desist from contacting our witnesses either those that are scheduled to appear or those that have already testified before the Court. We understand the Court's ruling on that. We think that inaction has now prompted the OTP to further contact this witness. It has frustrated our purposes in bringing forth witnesses not only this week but other witnesses that were scheduled to come throughout the Defence case. We again would just appeal to the Court that scheduling of witnesses does not happen overnight. The Defence has worked diligently and has brought forth as many witnesses as we could. Unfortunately, this circumstance has arisen. The Defence apologises to the Court and to the entire system if it has in some way inconvenienced that process. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before I give the floor to the Prosecution, I want to express the Bench's surprise that the question of calling witnesses is called now a question of short notice and not knowing beforehand. We discussed several times that, no doubt, it's for the Defence to prepare in due time proper proffers for the incoming witnesses. And as you have told us several times, it takes at least five days in advance to call a witness taking into account that a witness would need a "visum." So in conclusion, this means that already two weeks ago, when acting accurately, the Defence would and should have been able to give us the list of the witnesses to come for this week. And as we indicated in the scheduling order and as we indicated in the -- in open court, this Trial Chamber is no longer prepared to continue with that what we would call from objective point of view - I emphasise this - an obstruction of the Court proceedings. The parties should know that one case one day in court - I don't want to give the exact figure - but some thousands of dollars. And there is no right for any party to endanger these proceedings and thereby endangering the work of the entire Tribunal because no doubt also the other inmates of the Detention Unit have a right to have heard their case in due time. Or even endangering the entire system of international jurisdiction. I know that the Prosecution wants to answer, and we have time enough during this week apparently and unfortunately to do this sooner than expected in the absence of additional witnesses. But how can we believe that in the future, this will not happen again? And we will be confronted one week beforehand that no witness will be available. So in fact, until now, we can't see any proper justification. In the beginning, we learned from the Defence that the Defence believed that there would be a videolink this week. It reads from the transcript, and I reassured this, without any doubt that it takes two to three weeks in advance to have these videolinks prepared. I'm extremely grateful for the registry and especially Madam Dahuron that she took the necessary measures, especially related to translations, that we can have the videolink next week already. Without this exceptional assistance given by the registry, this wouldn't have been possible for the next week. But we don't know whether for the next week we can fill in the entire week by video witnesses only. Therefore, already now, my request to take care that at least one additional witness is available for the next week from the side of the Defence. 92 bis statements will be taken during even the weekend, and we appreciate these efforts from the Defence and, in addition, from the members of the -- or the people working for translation, for the registry, and especially Madam Dahuron. We will necessarily go once again through the list of witnesses during this week. You have already seen in our scheduling order that the Chamber, in order to facilitate and streamline the case, we went through the remaining witnesses and came to a certain conclusion that a number of witnesses from the perspective of the Bench in any event has to be heard live. Our invitation for the Prosecution is to be prepared when going through the witness list once again, to comment whether the Prosecution from the outset can tell us that they are not prepared to hear a witness under 92 bis and in order to avoid double workload, it would be appropriate that we hear this as soon as possible. In addition, we found that a number of witnesses appear to be repetitive, especially character witnesses. I hope that on the basis of the submissions of the Prosecution, we can agree that that what is expected to hear from these witnesses is already not only in evidence, but it is already proven and we don't have to go ahead with these character witnesses. And then at the same time, when lead counsel and chief of prosecution - I think the acting representatives of the Prosecution could this do even better having followed the entire case - could present their contribution to speed up the case as foreseen in the statute. This would mean to streamline the case by indicating what are the incidents they are believing that based on that what we have heard until now can no longer be proven. What are the charges the Prosecution may, under the impression of that what we have heard until now, is prepared to drop in whole or in part? I have to re-emphasise that already from a point of logic, you can't proceed at the same time with the prosecution of Dr. Stakic as the planner and the same time aider and abettor. We expect a clear word from the side of the Prosecution whether it's really their -- still their case that Dr. Stakic had the necessary intent required for charge 1. We expect a clear word, what about the relation of charge 7 and 8. We expect a clear word, what about the deprivation of fundamental rights as described in the amended indictment. Is it really still the Prosecution's case that they want to proceed on the basis of an infringement or deprivation of all these fundamental rights by Dr. Stakic as we can read it from the fourth amended indictment? Why do I mention this at this point in time? Because there are some truths in the contribution and submission by the Defence that when the case is not streamlined, they have a broader approach or a broader approach is necessary for them when interviewing witnesses during the examination-in-chief. And we could speed up, no doubt, when what I would call the duty and the obligation of the Prosecution they will finally tell us what at the end of the day is their case, and that it's easier for the Defence to know where are the weak points of their Defence, where do they have to add the one or other point of evidence. The word "evidence" in connection with the Prosecution brings me to another point. We did not yet decide - we heard only the response - to a motion to bar the documents S391, S392, and S393 from evidence. I think it's necessary to discuss this in open court, and proprio motu, we would like to add to the list of suddenly appearing documents the one document presenting -- presented by the Prosecution having even no 65 ter number but including a number of signatures, also allegedly the signature of Dr. Stakic, his deputy presented during the presence of Witness Vila. We need some explanation from the Prosecution why this late presenting the document, why not including this in Mr. ten Camp's expertise. And we would like what else will come in the future prolonging and endangering this case as we have experienced in the past under the late disclosure of the six statements of alleged members of the Crisis Staff of Prijedor. Finally, then, when it's the question of maybe sanctions against Defence counsel, I think it is not a question that time by time, Defence counsel agrees that this case will be concluded as envisaged. You know that we already once postponed the end of the Defence case already in July last year. We have to make a clear distinction between the rights of the accused and the duties and obligations of Defence counsel. In case Defence counsel would not live up to their obligations in due time, this Trial Chamber would not be able to conclude the case because no doubt Dr. Stakic in person has his own right that all the witnesses he believes can serve his own interests in defending himself have to be heard. And therefore, a shorter case without having heard all the necessary witnesses is no option at all. But let us now hear first of all, if you want to add something from your point of view, and then the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. I'll try to explain what happened in the field during the last week, Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday, when we tried to bring more witnesses for this week. First of all, we encountered a problem with the Witness Number 001 who didn't have a passport, and he was not able to get a passport during Thursday and Friday because of the holidays in Bosnia. Witness Number 006 was willing to come two weeks ago, but he cannot come now before the 27th of February because he is a manager in his company, and there is a final tax report in Bosnia due 27th of February, so he cannot leave. We contacted again Witness Number 013 whom we report that has throat cancer and the situation is still the same. So we are trying to find a replacement. Witness 034 left for the US, and we couldn't contact him at all. Witness 041, his brother died the last week, so he was not able to travel. Witness 055, we couldn't locate at all. Witness 083 still hasn't gotten his permission from his superiors because he's a priest. 084 is a lady, and her husband is now objecting her testimony because this lady spoke with Ms. Nada Markovska and learned about her troubles with the Prosecution. So her husband is not allowing her to testify now. And we couldn't locate Witness 089. So those are basically the witnesses we planned to call aside from the witnesses who would testify via videolink. We also contacted Witness Number 058, the witness who was here previously. He is still sick. I spoke with him. He said that he has to take at least for another ten days the medications, and he told me that he doesn't feel well. Our investigator is trying today also to provide at least two additional witnesses if possible to arrange it with the Victims and Witness Unit to have them on Thursday and Friday, but we cannot promise it. And we also have to contact this investigator regarding our 92 bis motion. So we are really trying our best - maybe it's not enough. And we know that we two weeks ago, we should have organised this, but we were really thinking at that time that we would have those two witnesses from the Crisis Staff. And maybe that's our mistake that we didn't put enough effort to bring the witnesses for this week. So we want to apologise once again, and we want to tell you that we'll try again to have witnesses for the Thursday and Friday. But again, it's not only up to us. It's up to the Victims and Witness Unit who are helping -- really helping us a lot. But it's also not only up to them; they have to ask the assistance of the embassies. So sometimes it's time-consuming, but still we think that we'll be able to bring somebody at least for Friday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I really appreciate your comments. And as regards witnesses, maybe witnesses for Thursday and Friday, I want to invite you to ask for the assistance of the Chamber if necessary when there should be obstacles or impediments, be it in the Victims and Witnesses Unit. I know they are doing whatever they can, but maybe we can also be of assistance by contacting the one or other embassy. And also, to make this quite clear, you may have seen this during the last week, it is not only possible but it is necessary in these cases to contact the Judges directly, and we are no longer prepared to follow rules that are not written in, be it the statute, or be the Rules of Procedure and Evidence not allowing for direct contacts with the Judges, especially the Presiding Judge. We will ourself in principle when it's urgent contact you directly, and this is true for both parties. And to whom it may concern, whenever you want to have a dispute or not an agreement with rulings of the Chamber, please do not contact and dispute with legal officers of this Chamber, but please directly with the Chamber. So now for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's a number of issues that Your Honour raised. First, in regards to the exhibits not on the 65 ter list and the three exhibits in particular that were the subject of the Defence motion, I believe Your Honours did get our written response which was filed last Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: That's true. But when discussing this, we would like to hear in addition the comments on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. As to all of these documents, Your Honour, we have the same comment, and that is that the rules require us -- are very specific about what our disclosure obligations are. Rule 65 ter states that the Prosecution is obligated to provide the Defence with a copy of all exhibits it intends to use at the time that it files - and this is filed at the time that the pre-trial brief is filed before the case begins. Similarly, with symmetry, the Defence when they file their pre-trial brief at the close of the Prosecution case, they also file a list of documents they intend to use. During the Prosecution case, the Defence may bring up documents that obviously are not on its 65 ter list because it hadn't yet been filed. We believe the Prosecution has a similar right and nothing in the rules preclude us from presenting to a witness a document that we did not intend to use at the time we filed the pre-trial brief, but which becomes relevant. You have us have learned a tremendous amount about what happened in Prijedor, and the issues in this case have focussed tremendously since the pre-trial brief was filed. For example, this issue of these three documents, the issue was raised by the Defence witness that officers of non-Serbian ethnicity were not -- were allowed to remain in the army and there was no policy against that, and these documents specifically go to contradict that testimony. The document that Your Honour raised this morning, I don't have it in front of me, but as I recall, that was a document that was during the testimony of Mr. Vila, it was brought out because Mr. Vila was one of the signatories. At the time the pre-trial brief was filed, the Prosecution did not know that Mr. Vila would testify for the Defence. The significance and relevance of that document, it became more relevant when Mr. Vila testified and it could be put to him and he could be asked if that was his signature. We had no idea Mr. Vila was going to testify at that time. The -- I don't recall now specifically what the document referred to, but I don't believe it was the actual contents of the decision or the list that was of significance; it was simply the signatures which have become more significant during the trial. We also recognised at that time the signature of Mr. Savanovic, that it was very similar to one of the signatures signed "Za" that was in dispute regarding -- that has the typed name of Dr. Stakic. So the rules only require the Prosecution to provide documents on the 65 ter list that it intends to use. And we filed a list with over 800 documents. We didn't use them all. We made our best effort to determine at that time what would be relevant. Some documents have become more relevant since then particularly based upon the Defence case. During the Defence case, items are going to come up that we did not anticipate at the time we filed our pre-trial brief. I can move on to another issue unless Your Honour has questions on that. As to the 92 bis statements, we would be happy to go through them, but I had a phone conversation with Mr. Ostojic last week, and he can correct me if I misinterpreted him, but my understanding is that the 92 bis statements that the Defence proposes will all be of witnesses that we do not have proffers for right now. These are new witnesses. So I called him to see if we could go through the proffers of which witnesses to see if the Prosecution would have an objection, and I believe he indicated that these were being -- he was in process of doing them, but they would all be new witnesses. But we would be happy to do that, and we are going to take a very cooperative attitude with the Court and with the Defence to try to get as many witnesses admitted by 92 bis as possible as long as they fit the definition of 92 bis, which is the testimony does not go to the acts or conduct of the accused. In that case, it's not a question of discretion by the Prosecution or the Court that is not admissible under 92 bis. That's a prerequisite for the statement to come in. As to the Prosecution streamlining the case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I just interrupt because this question should be discussed, and I think it was once again quite clear, that in our decision as from the 12th of February, we indicated that it would be necessary to have a list of those witnesses where the Defence believes that their testimony could be admitted under Rule 92 bis. And no doubt, it's mandatory that they have the testimony has to fulfill all the prerequisites under 92 bis, especially 92 bis(A). And therefore, we still expect, and this is due in two hours, that a list of these witnesses who -- a list of the witnesses whose statement the Defence intends to introduce by way of Rule 92 bis, along with a detailed description of the areas that will be covered by each witness in his or her Rule 92 bis statement. And then it would be not within -- between the parties but in open court to be discussed whether or not these witnesses, in fact, can be heard under Rule 92 bis. So as soon as possible and as soon as practicable, we have to discuss this. I don't know whether the Defence is prepared to have this document filed before 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It will be filed at or around 12.00, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As a kind of -- as an act of courtesy, we could receive courtesy copies in advance. This would be of assistance for our further proceedings that we as soon as possible can go through this list and thereby have a common approach from the side of the Bench and then let's hear also the submissions of the Prosecution. But no doubt, and I was a little bit -- not only a little bit surprised, but maybe even shocked to hear that these would be new witnesses, not on the list already. Can you please comment on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I can, I think, Your Honour. The 92 bis witnesses after discussion on at least three occasions with the OTP will be those allowed under the rules in our view that go specifically on three issues: One issue relates to cumulative evidence which we believe has already been brought forth both during the OTP case and the Defence case on some issues. The second issue goes to character as the Court pointed out and reputation of Dr. Stakic. Without having to call the witnesses live, we believe that the 92 bis statements will satisfactorily give the Court and Dr. Stakic ample evidence to clearly depict him and his character and reputation at or around the time of the indictment. Third, we believe goes unfortunately we're compelled, and I must stress this as attorneys, to address the issue of mitigation. Under the rules, I believe it's our duty, although perhaps in the general view of things inconsistent with how the procedures personally I view that we bring forth some mitigation and some testimony or 92 bis statements relating to mitigation. The Defence under no circumstances wants this Court, and we recognise that this Court sees this in the rules and does not take our comments on the mitigation to suggest that we are conceding any points in the indictment, and we will address that both in our oral arguments as well as in our final brief. However, it's our duty as set forth in the rules to bring forth such mitigation evidence which we believe we will be able to bring forth by way of 92 bis. Quite candidly, the witnesses, some if not the majority of them, are new from the witness list, but not new to the OTP. They are in part family members of Dr. Stakic. I specifically in my conversation with the OTP identified some if not all of the witnesses that we expect will give their 92 bis statements. We are prepared and will be prepared at noon or soon after the break to give the Court and to discuss in detail each of those 92 bis witnesses, and we believe and are confident that the Court will accept them all as 92 bis witnesses. Again, we've streamlined the number of witnesses from our initial list because we believe the evidence warrants it and the case in its current proceeding dictates that we streamline the case. We likewise believe that the 92 bis witnesses should be accepted as set forth in our motion. And for the three reasons identified in the rules, cumulative evidence, reputation, character, and mitigation, just to summarise. I would like also just to address the issue of our motion and the response by the OTP on the documents that we consider to be improperly offered during the Defence case. But I await the Court's instruction on when you'd like me to discuss that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think this can be done in the context of also the Prosecution's submission to the question of streamlining and not continuing to obstruct the ongoing case. Maybe when we have heard the witness, and I learned from the so-called lead counsel of the Prosecution, that she intends to appear together with the head of Prosecutions within the OTP on Wednesday. I think this is then the appropriate point in time. What we have to do now and maybe even today is to first to go through your list you want to prepare, and then to go through the list, the remaining list, of witnesses, whether or not the one or other can be either struck from the list or can also be admitted under 92 bis. I think this is mandatory that we can take the necessary provision, especially Madam Dahuron for the preparation of the weekend. This has absolute priority, and we should do this today. Let's come back to the question of this late disclosure of -- or presentation of documents once again later because there seems from the side of the Prosecution a kind of misunderstanding. No doubt, these proceedings here in the Tribunal are first of all those copied from common-law systems, but we all are aware that there is a hybrid set of Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and these gaps have to be filled from the international point of view. And the Prosecution should be aware that the Bench has to act in a more stronger and stricter way than in a mere common-law system. We have the right to put questions to the witnesses. We are under the obligation to put questions to witnesses. We are under the obligation to call witnesses. And it may be, as said by the Appeals Chamber in Kupreskic, even be an error in law if we would not hear proprio motu the one or other witness. Therefore, it's not the Prosecution being alone, the one in this courtroom being in possession and having the own and only right to dictate which parts of evidence can be presented here and there. No doubt that those documents already from the perspective of the fourth amended indictment - I'm discussing now the three documents - would have been of importance, not only relevance. And especially we cannot disguise our clear disappointment that the Prosecution failed when we discussed what to include in Mr. ten Camp's expertise these important, maybe important, document we only received during the testimony of Mr. Vila more or less by chance. But we have to return to these issues later during this week. I interrupted the Prosecution when Mr. Koumjian just was to discuss a question of how to streamline best the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I intended to address the Court's issue as to counts and modes of responsibility. Your Honour, the Prosecution is not proceeding on any count or any mode of responsibility that we do not believe we can prove to this Chamber by evidence and that evidence has already been presented to prove these counts and these modes of responsibility. We do not know how the Chamber will rule. We cannot be assured about which mode of responsibility, which counts, the Court will find proven beyond a reasonable doubt and obviously the Court cannot give us that assurance. This mode of -- or this practice of filing charges in the alternative or different counts has been approved in the Tribunal. It was approved in this case when the indictment was confirmed, when the indictment was challenged, and the indictment -- form of the indictment was allowed. And in the 98 bis decision. For example, let me go to counts 7 and 8. Counts 7 and 8 we believe are clearly distinct in the law. Count 7 deals with deportation over a national border which we know occurred in this case. Many of our witnesses, particularly those early in the case, testified from the Manjaca camp to being taken to Croatia, and I think we even have a newspaper article where Dr. Stakic is quoted regarding these convoys. Count 8 deals with the internal forcible transfer. There does seem to be a distinction in the law between internal forcible transfer and deportation. The way I understand the law, deportation under our statute does not cover forcing someone over the border from what was the territory of Republika Srpska to the territory controlled by Muslim or Croat forces. And this happened. This is not an academic question. This happened to thousands, thousand of people in Prijedor. I recall many of the witnesses who testified about the trip to Travnik trying to get them to shorten their answer and they wouldn't stop talking about what that experience was like being on those convoys walking across the front lines in the night seeing wheelchairs taken -- carried over rocks going around mine fields. One person said stepping on a piece of human flesh. This is not an academic question, and we believe that it's a very important question for international law and for -- because it happens not only in Bosnia, it happens brought the world. It has happened throughout history. It happened in the Second World War, in the Soviet Union, and in many other places, in the Ottoman empire. It's a very, very important issue, and it happened in this case. And we believe there is no reason for us to drop that -- and it would set a very bad precedent for us to drop that count. Furthermore, as for genocide, we believe that the evidence shows that thousands of people were killed in a period from basically late May through early August, to the end of August. So a period of basically three months in a town that was pretty small. It was about 50.000 non-Serbs according to the Defence; that number is actually much smaller because many had left. That's a huge percentage of people. We do not believe that Dr. Stakic was unaware of going on. We think the evidence shows that he had to be aware of what was going on and he actively participated in that. We think the evidence shows that the only reasonable conclusion is he did have the intent to destroy that group in whole or in part. Further, we understand the issue of the intent of genocide is a very complicated legal issue. I could address that. To do justice, it would probably take me more than an hour certainly to address the legal aspects of joint criminal enterprise and the intents necessary for aiding and abetting for joint criminal enterprise. I don't think the Court wants to hear a final argument now. But I can say on behalf of every single member of the team of the OTP on this case, we believe we've proven the charges, and we're proceeding because we believe ethically we are required to because this is what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I appreciate your comments. Maybe in fact not to have a kind of deadlock, it can be necessary that it might be seen as a second 98 bis decision, we have to discuss as soon as possible and as we said already earlier during the Defence case in the case of absence of a witness, we should discuss legal issues. And therefore, I invite the parties to be prepared to discuss these legal questions, especially the question which is extremely difficult for the Defence, the question of joint criminal enterprise, who were members of this joint criminal enterprise. This brings us to the question of the testimony of Ms. Plavsic, who apparently we didn't receive any response by counsel of Madam Plavsic right now. But apparently what we have seen in the other case Prosecutor versus Biljana Plavsic, there is a limited likelihood that she will testify in this case. And as stated earlier, before there is a final judgement in her case, this Trial Chamber does not intend to compel a still-accused person to testify. It would only be possible if a person is already convicted, and then it would be another legal situation. Therefore, let's try to proceed in the following order: Let us start today with Witness 070. Let us hear what are the impediments to hear the witnesses maybe foreseen for Thursday and Friday that we can overcome the maybe obstacles. Let us today go through the list of the former witnesses and the new witnesses on the basis of the statement given by the Defence later this day. Let us then go through the offered documents by the Defence during the last witness's testimony. We have not decided yet on their -- on the admission into evidence of these documents. We have to do this, also taking into account that we have to decide either on request or proprio motu whether this witness has to come to The Hague a second time. And then let's continue to discuss some legal issues, and I think the Prosecution did understand very well that it's not the question here related to -- especially to count 8, Mr. Koumjian addressed right now. It's a question of general principles of criminal law, and you find in the late decisions of this Tribunal a different approach to this open clause of "other inhumane acts." And maybe based on judicial hints related to this whether or not maybe is the distinction made in the past between deportation and forcible transfer is not the correct approach. Maybe you have seen, for example, that in the ICC statute, you have a different approach where you would include forcible transfer in deportation and, of course, this has to be discussed that the Defence is able to prepare their Defence case. So let's continue in this order. Are there any other submissions by the parties in the moment? Please, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, thank you. We accept the Court's invitation for assistance on this one issue and on all issues obviously. It relates to the documents that the Defence submitted in October or November of 2002. We submitted in our exhibit list the specific articles and captioned -- identified specifically the article which we wanted to have translated, and we thought there was ample time. In January of this year, we were advised that we needed to highlight each and every article so that there would be no confusion as to which article would be translated. Although on the specific page, as the Court has received, we believe, and the OTP, the article headline is referred to, and clearly identified in the article. Nevertheless, we would like the Court, if at all possible, to somehow give us assistance or guidance as to how we can get that department here in the Tribunal to expedite the translation of the documents that we've submitted. In part, they have completed some relating to Kozarski Vjesnik. However, all the documents are not done. We do not have any recourse to speed the process and would accept the Court's invitation to the extent possible if the Court can assist us in expediting the translation of those documents. We also have a request with respect - and it's an ongoing request - with respect to outstanding Kozarski Vjesnik articles and publications in March, April, and May of 1992. That has not ever been forwarded to us, although our requests were made. Other articles and periodicals were submitted to us, however those remain outstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As mentioned previously, we would invite the Defence to present those documents already translated, already in the English translation related to the document tendered, the second-last week, it's our intention to let those parts of those documents in B/C/S if not yet identified by the Prosecution as already translated in another case, that these would be read out as we did it previously from the booth, and thereby we would have access to the documents and thereby we can rule whether or not it's necessary to hear this witness a second time. And finally, if you could please be so kind and give the legal officer the name of the person you're in contact with related to the question of translations. Thank you. Any further submissions by the side of the Prosecution in the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We do have one other, I'm sorry, Your Honour. Actually two others, if I may with the one I think appears logically. Your Honour, our request with respect to Exhibit 375 which was admitted on the last day of the OTP's case on September 27th, 2002, during that session, which was in open session, there was a discussion with the Court in connection with Exhibit S375A, and it was our understanding at that time as reflected on page 8.923 of the transcript of September 27th, 2002, that the B/C/S version of the article that purports to translate S375A would be forthcoming to us. That request has not been fulfilled, and we again orally would request the Court to compel the OTP to give us the article in which they through lines 13 through 18 tell us that they will certainly give us the B/C/S version of the document. Again, the page for the Court's reference is 8.923.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's not necessary to compel the OTP. The OTP will do this without any doubt it's on our to-do list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have the quote in front of me, but we do not have a B/C/S version of this article. I thought I -- I don't know what exactly -- what words exactly were used at that time. But this is a translation from a service that translates articles. The original would have been in B/C/S. I believe it's from the SRNA news service if I recall. And this translation comes from a service that monitors foreign broadcasts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But if you could be so kind and revisit this question, I think it would be helpful because, in fact, it is also on our to-do list.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And finally, if I may, Your Honour, just to reiterate our request with respect to Kozarski Vjesnik, on February 24th of 2000, the Defence requested that the articles relating to the issues dated April through May of 1992 be presented to us. Whether the Defence and the investigators checked with the institution which holds those documents, we were informed that all copies were taken by SFOR in 1997. There are none in existence, and we believe that it does go to the -- some merits of the fourth amended indictment. We can share with the Court the response by the Kozarski Vjesnik where they say that this was -- all the copies were taken by SFOR in 1997, and we would once again request that the OTP provide us with copies in full of those articles for those pertinent periods of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before I ask the OTP to answer, we would from our perspective add one additional request to produce evidence under Rule 98, and this would be please check if the quote is correct, the Official Gazette of Serbian Republic 3/92 where one should be able to find the constitution. And I think the OTP should have this document available in English and in B/C/S as well. I think for the purposes of our case, it's mandatory to have these legal documents at hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just briefly, on the Kozarski Vjesniks, I understand that when the Defence looked through what we had thought at the time were all of the issues that we had, they indicated that they were missing April and May. A second search was done. Ms. Karper reminds me, and on the 6th of December, we gave them what we could find from April and May. And I don't believe we have anything else. I'm hesitant to say that because these articles are held in various parts of the OTP. It was disclosures number 1233 to 1238. I would also point out, I know often in Prijedor places like that the answer when you first asked for documents is that they were taken by SFOR. But I do recall the testimony was that the Soros foundation, one of our witnesses pointed out, in Sarajevo does have copies of some Kozarski Vjesniks. And in fact, some of the copies that were put in recently that we had were obtained indirectly from the Soros foundation. So what we are missing may be held there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But nevertheless, I believe it's worthwhile once again revisiting your database whether there are in the meantime additional copies of Kozarski Vjesnik and, as mentioned, we would like to have introduced the Official Gazette of the Serbian Republic 3/92 in order to have the constitution. I can't see any other requests in the moment. This would mean that the time is ripe for having the break. Immediately after the break, we should hear the first witness. May I ask as usual, any protective measures necessary for Witness 070?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No protective measures, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then I would ask the usher to bring in the witness before the Bench is arriving. The trial stays adjourned until 11.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Good morning, Mr. Prastalo. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May we then, please, hear your solemn declaration. Would you please stand up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You may be seated. The floor is for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Prastalo.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My name is Branko Lukic, and together with John Ostojic, I represent Dr. Stakic before this Tribunal. Will you please for the record state your full name.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: Zoran Prastalo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I know this is not a usual thing to ask, but I would like to please ask you to make a brief pause every time you finished answering a question so that the interpretation can catch up with you. Furthermore, if it strikes you as strange that I should pause after you've given your answer, this doesn't mean that I'm not satisfied with your answer but I'm also waiting for the interpretation to catch up. For the record, will you please state your father's name.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: Boro.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When were you born, Mr. Prastalo?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: On the 25th of October, 1960.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: Ljubija, Prijedor Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where do you reside today?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: In Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did you reside in 1992 -- 1991 and 1992, can you please tell us?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: In Ljubija and in Prijedor. Until 1991, I lived in Ljubija where I was born and where I finished elementary school. I went to secondary school in Prijedor. I worked for a while in Ljubija, and then for a while in Prijedor. After that, I went to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did your family reside, I mean your wife and children, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: In Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were born and you grew up in Ljubija. Can you please tell us about the ethnic makeup of Ljubija prior to the outbreak of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: Ljubija was a predominantly Muslim town. Serbs amounted to about 10 per cent of the total population of Ljubija, and Croats, around 8 per cent. It was a workers' town. We all lived there, and most of the people had jobs which were somehow related to the iron ore mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have friends who belonged to all the different ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: Yes. I was working for an electric and technical company where we had 70 per cent Muslim work force, between 10 and 15 per cent of the work force were Croats, and between 10 and 15 per cent were Serbs. I practiced sports actively, too, in my place of birth. I played football, and I played for FC Ljubija where we had the same ratio more or less. There was nothing you could do about that. It was just the makeup of the population in the place where I lived. We lived there. We socialised with one another. We worked together. We would visit each other for holidays, religious holidays, Bajram. That's about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In April of 1992, where were you working at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: In April of 1992 -- well, actually since 1990 -- between 1990 and 1992, I worked for the Hidroflex company, Prijedor. It was the first privately-owned enterprise which opened in Prijedor. We produced a high-pressure tubes and cables, hydraulic tubes and cables. When I worked in Prijedor, I would travel back to Ljubija to my home. That's as far as work is concerned. The Hidroflex company. I left the electrotechnical combine where I had been working up until that point in 1990, and then I joined this privately-owned enterprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your wife and children, did they visit in April or May?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: Yes. My wife and children came to see my parents in Ljubija. On that day, when I finished work, sometimes I would leave work late because I did a lot of travelling all over the place. So I would come home sometimes very late. That particular day, I returned home about 5.00 or half past 5.00 in the afternoon. In Donja Ljubija, we used to refer to the village as the railway station, because that's what the bus stop was called. Two roads forked there, one of the roads turns off left to the village of Ljubija, and then the other road turns to Gornja Ljubija where I lived. I was stopped by the police. They pulled my car over. And the policeman on duty was a friend of mine. We used to play football together, Muhamed Odobasic from Ljubija. He told me to get out of the car, and he wanted to see my documents. I gave him my documents. I opened the trunk. He searched the car, and he searched me, too. A policeman, a traffic policeman from Prijedor named Sarajlic was standing by watching, which struck me as slightly strange. I can't remember his first name. I think it's Ismet, but I'm not sure. He just stood there and watched. I knew both of the men. Ismet owned a cafe in Donja Ljubija, a cafe that I visited quite frequently. As I said before, there were both Serbs, Muslims, in Prijedor, and my family likewise -- in my family, I had members of other ethnic groups also. My family is a mixed one. So they told me, it's okay, you can leave. I asked them what the whole thing was about. I thought that something had happened, something else. And they said, No, but from now on things are going to be slightly different and not the way they used to be up until now. I didn't understand that, so I came home. I was feeling not quite at peace, so I didn't believe anything like that could happen since I was aware of the ethnic makeup. I took my wife and my children to Prijedor, and then several months later, my wife left for Belgrade. I continued working regularly. I would go to Ljubija, go back to Ljubija, but I no longer returned home that late. I tried not to. And I didn't go back that often. I had a flat, my sister's flat, that I could use to sleep over, and I would normally take that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us when this event you told us about took place exactly, if you could remember the date or approximately when it occurred.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: That was just after the 1st of May. I think it was about the 10th of May, because there was the 1st of May celebration, and I think the event took place about the 10th of May. These were active-duty policemen. My friend Muhamed Odobasic, we used to play football together which made the whole thing even more curious for me. His sister and his brother-in-law who were Muslims, they lived, they stayed at my place privately. If I may just add the following: My mother -- sister's brother-in-law, she would baby sit their child when they were working. And she was providing for both the food and the rent getting nothing or asking nothing in return.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why did you get your wife and children and take them to Prijedor? Did you feel unsafe?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: I did feel unsafe. I tried to comfort myself saying that nothing would come of it, but still, I had certain fears because the war in Slavonia had already begun, and I was afraid that something bad would happen to my family. And that was the sole reason why I decided to move my children and my wife to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just for the sake of the transcript, were your wife and children already living in Belgrade at that time, and then were visiting Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Let me just explain the following, why my wife and children lived in Belgrade. In 1990, as I've said, I left a state or socially-owned enterprise, and some of my friends and relatives approved of this. But certain members of my family, because my father had worked for 40 years at the iron ore mine, they were not great believers in private initiative, but I was. So I joined the privately-owned company because the conditions were better. And it was a challenge to work with people who saw things more or less the way I did, and I don't think I made a mistake. In Prijedor since 1992 [as interpreted], it was impossible to work, it was impossible to really earn money in the line of work that we were in. It was very difficult to work. The market was not functioning really well across the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My apologies. Just for the transcript, did you say in 1991 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you said it was impossible to work due to the nonfunctioning of the market.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue. This was only a correction for the transcript, because the transcript reflected 1992, and I thought you had said 1991.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: In 1991, it was very difficult to work. I took my family to Belgrade, moved my family to Belgrade, because I didn't own a flat. And I was also thinking about that. I was afraid that the situation would go wrong, and I thought I must see to it that I have a flat to live in and put my family in. My son and my daughter were very small, very young. And in Belgrade, I put my family up in a private flat that I had rented. I stayed, and I kept on residing in Prijedor. I worked in Prijedor too. Every two or three months, I would visit my family. We would speak to each other on the phone. That was about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said it was almost impossible to work in Prijedor. Why do you say that? Can you please explain.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: When communists fell from power, I know that -- I personally know that everyone was in favour of the communists leaving and of setting up national parties of which I myself was never a supporter. I was never a member of any party because no party was aware of the economic issues. They were national parties. And it was my understanding that this just wouldn't work, and I was proven right eventually. As far as Prijedor Municipality, my municipality, is concerned, we had the Municipal Assembly set up. And there was a lot of obstruction. And I myself experienced some obstruction, too. Land was -- there was a claim for land to be bought up so that the first privately-owned factory could be built. Dragan Popovic was the investigator and Hidroflex was the company and I worked for him and. And we were, in a manner of speaking, partners. Dragan Popovic was a Croat. Some people from the municipality simply wouldn't talk to us. I can go as far as to say that they lied to us. I'm talking now about deputies, deputies of the SDA, because they believed that Dragan Popovic was a Serb by nationality when, in fact, he was a Croat. His father's name is Ilija, and his mother's name is Milica. This person now lives both in Rijeka -- works in Rijeka and lives in Prijedor. I tried to reach the president of the municipality on a number of occasions; however, either the president was busy or he was away or he was in a meeting so that I had no way of getting in touch with the president of the municipality. I never spoke about this to the president. I did speak to several people who were deputies, I had been told. One of them was either from Trnopolje or from Kozarusa - I can't remember - but he was not really in a position to help me. On that occasion, I was outraged, and I insisted that someone from the municipality see me. The vice-president of the Municipal Assembly was Dr. Milomir Stakic at that time. I had heard of him, but I had never seen up to that point. He agreed to see me. I spoke to him about my problem. The main problem was for the request to go straight to the Municipal Assembly because neither the president of the municipality nor the Executive Board could deal with that. It just simply had to be put on the agenda so that there could be a discussion and votes whether land should be sold to this privately-owned company who declared itself ready to buy this land. Mr. Stakic, and I could hardly believe it, agreed to see us. He talked to us, but he couldn't promise anything. He said he would see what he could do. He said he welcomed our initiative. We explained what we were after. We had all the plans. And after a while, this did finally reach the Municipal Assembly, our request. And at a session of the Municipal Assembly, it was decided that the land should be given to us, so we managed to obtain it. However, when we had to receive the decision from the Municipal Assembly, once they found out, they simply voted in an ignorant manner only to get it over with. I'm not sure what item on the agenda it was. I think the 40th or the 41st item of the agenda so that the deputies voted in favour. But I don't think they were focussed enough to know what they were voting. The next day, however, the president of the municipality started an initiative to stop the whole thing, and he asked that the decision not be granted us. To cut the long story short, we did get this decision from the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly through the usual and regular channels. And after that, in record time, I dare say, within 90 days, we built a factory which is still there which had Serbs, Muslims, and Croats as its employees. I could give you names if you would like me to. Qualified people were leaving state-owned or socially-owned companies. One of them was Senad, who was a technical production director. In our company, there was Jasna Cehic, head of finances. I myself was the deputy of the owner, a partner you might say. So there were all different structures working together in that enterprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us until when you stayed in that enterprise. What happened? Did you ever go to Croatia during the war to see Mr. Dragan Popovic, the owner?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: Times were hard, as I said, so it was difficult to travel. I tried to do what I could. I kept on working. I tried to keep things as they were when Mr. Popovic left the whole thing to us. He left, but it's important to point out that he was working on the building of another factory in Rijeka in Croatia. So in 1990 and 1991, he started building the factory in Rijeka, which is still there. We had a plan, and we had a shop in Zagreb, like a branch office, and in Sisak in Croatia, another one. And before, that we had one in Dvor na Uni. I did meet him several times. I would simply inform him of the way the enterprise was going, what we were up to. I met him in Hungary several times, too. His own investment was a financial failure. He overinvested in a manner of speaking, so he had nothing left to live on because he had invested too much of his own money. So he ran out of money to keep his family. I left through Republika Srpska, Serbia, Hungary, and Slovenia, and through Ilirska Bistrica, I entered Croatia. I brought him his own money which we had made by selling the goods produced by the factory. We bought our raw materials mostly from Germany. I travelled to Germany to buy them there, and so on. At the factory, we had quite a lot of money in stock put on the side, between 2 and 3 million German mark, which had to be preserved. We had to keep producing. We had to keep giving people their salaries. We paid people their salaries regularly, and we paid the tax, too, to the state. That's about it. Since I was speaking about the enterprise, perhaps I should finish. I may leave the time frame we are talking about, but there was something else that was important that happened, too. While I was still down there, I enjoyed the support of the illegally-elected government. I hadn't requested anything. The only thing I had requested was to keep on working normally. When there was a changeover in Prijedor when one government left and one government arrived, and now I am speaking about the Serbian government, I ran into significant problems because the new government - and I am convinced of what I'm saying - was much more radical than the previous one. Certain decisions of the Executive Board -- pursuant to certain decisions of the Executive Board, they came to take my property away. They said it was the property of the Municipal Assembly, and there was nothing I could do about it, whether I had all the documents, whether I was aware of that. So I kept struggling as much as I could. Through the media, through Radio Prijedor and the local newspaper, Kozarski Vjesnik, this went on for about five months.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. When the attack of the Serb radical government started against you to take the factory from you, when did that start?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: That started already when they were not in power. I socialised with a lot of people, with Croats, Muslims, and others. I can tell you more about it later on. I socialised with everybody, with the opposition as well as they call themselves. They would tell me why these people are in power. I knew some of these people. I went to school with some of them. And they simply told me this is Ustasha property, and we are going to take it. This has to be Serbian, and the Serbian flag has to be put up on your factory. They really did what they threatened to do, but they did it only for seven years --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: They took over the factory for seven days, the interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: For seven days. I didn't leave the factory for seven days. When they took power, they started doing this, starting with September of that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What year was that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: That was September 1992. And when they took power, they realised their ideas. They first sent a messenger from the Municipal Assembly with a decision. I didn't want to take the decision because to my mind, that decision was illegal, and the decision was that we should move out from the factory and hand over our private company to the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor. And as I've already said, this was one of the first private factories in the whole area. After that, another decision followed which was issued by the Executive Board to the police, and then the police handed that decision over to me. Again, I didn't want to take it. I didn't want to leave the factory, and the only ally I had were the media. I didn't fear for my life. I didn't fear for the life of my family because my family was in Belgrade. The only thing that I had was the factory, and if that was taken away -- if that had been taken away from me, they would have taken everything from me. And it lasted for some four or five months. Finally, I had word that Mr. Popovic, and I agreed that we should accept another private company in Prijedor together with Hidroflex. So we merged with this other company. We managed to do that. It took seven to eight months of struggle after which we managed to keep our factory. Let me just tell you something more about this company, give you some indicators of its work. In that company, to this very day, the owner is still the same, and it is still the same private owner who has a company in Rijeka and another one in Sisak. At that time, we worked together. We did not pay too much attention to territories. He has a company in Bihac. We did business with Karlovac, Bihac, Belgrade. We were not interested in territory; the only thing we were interested in was business and business success.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please clarify one thing. Who impersonated that group which started to take your company already in September 1992? Who was that who epitomised that group?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: There were a few people who wanted power. I always believed that they were not capable. They were not fit to be in power, because they never did anything for our town or for themselves. The only thing that they managed to do for themselves was to appoint their own directors of various companies. Whatever they could plunder, they plundered. I can say that openly. They appointed a person in the position of director of Energopetrol. After some time, it turned out that it was known publicly that some 450.000 to 500.000 German marks had been embezzled. The hardest moment for our town when these -- this money should have been used to purchase petrol that was badly needed for sowing. Some companies were confiscated by the mere fact that people who were appointed in top positions were not skilled and qualified to discharge those duties. So besides the difficult situation that prevailed in the economy, the situation was even aggravated by the appointment of people who were not fit to be in the top positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I just stop you for a moment. I think it would be helpful for all of us in order not to come back to this area if you would (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Confirmed. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prastalo, I would also like to clarify some things with you. You said that this group started already in September, but when was it that the thing was followed through? Was it in 1992 in September or sometime later?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: No, the whole thing was never really followed through. Nothing happened after that day. They tried to do something already in September and things started developing sometime before new year's or in January. It lasted -- everything lasted for a long time. And it -- to my mind, it lasted -- it felt like a century. I didn't go to town. I kept a very low profile. I was afraid because this was not my personal property. I wanted to protect it and to keep it. So when I said that they tried to do something, they started in September, and then the pressure continued more actively after November and lasted for seven or eight months, like I've said before. I can't remember exactly the dates. I only know that -- I can't even say exactly whether my media campaign lasted for five or six months, but this can be verified. It was the first time that somebody put up fight against these people. There were different titles in the media. I tried to give as good as I got, but that can all be verified in the media. That will be that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just another thing that I would like to clarify if I may, these efforts to take over the factory, did they in any way involve Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: No, I've already said that Dr. Stakic received me in his office. I didn't originally want to see Dr. Stakic. I wanted to see Mr. Cehajic. My attempts failed on some dozen occasions. Mr. Cehajic never saw me. It was his secretary who would always make excuses for Dr. Cehajic. She would say well, he's not here. He is in a meeting. He is with a delegation. After all these failed attempts, I went to see Dr. Stakic who at the time was the vice-president of the Municipal Assembly. He didn't make any promises to me. He just told me what the procedure was, and I knew what the procedure was. I knew exactly that the whole matter had to be put on the agenda and that deputies should be asked to vote either for or against. I presented the problem to Dr. Stakic, and I also told him that Mr. Popovic was a Croat. He did not see that as a problem. He helped me as much as he could to have this issue put on the agenda of the session of the Municipal Assembly. He was the only one who was happy to see us. I did not have anybody else's support. He was the first one who gave us any sort of support. And from then on, we started to -- I can't say exactly socialise, but from that time I started respecting this person who showed respect for a private initiative, who was ready to fight for our cause, and eventually we managed to build this factory and start operating. With Dr. Stakic, we didn't have any problems. We only had problems after we got the decision because Mr. Cehajic exerted influence on his people who were supposed to physically issue the decision. As for Dr. Stakic, he received us. He didn't make any promises, but he helped us with putting this issue on the agenda of a session of the Municipal Assembly. And finally it was at this session of the Municipal Assembly that it was voted in favour of this land, this building land being sold to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just another question before the break: Despite the disapproval of Dr. Cehajic who was the president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor, you eventually got the decision?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise. The question was not clear, I understand. What I'm saying is that even despite Dr. Cehajic's disapproval for this land to be sold to you - and Dr. Cehajic at the time was the president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor - eventually this was approved, this purchase of the land was approved?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: Yes, it was approved. We had to -- we had a certain delay in obtaining the decision. Once they realised that the land had been sold to Mr. Popovic, they stalled a little. It lasted some ten days for us to receive the decision. There was another meeting of the Executive Board that had to finally approve for the decision to be issued to us. But all this was due to the fact that everybody in Prijedor believed that Dragan Popovic was a Serb by ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would it be a convenient time, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until 1.30, but we would appreciate to receive the copies via the legal officer. Thank you. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.01 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Lukic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prastalo, can we continue now, please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will ask you something about the period between the 30th of April and the 30th of September, 1992. We have already referred to this period among others. You spoke about the period of time surrounding the 10th of May, 1992, when you were stopped at a checkpoint in Ljubija. Do you know if the police station in Ljubija at one moment split off from the public security station in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that. The incident that I spoke about also indicated this. I know that the main advocates of that were the people I've already spoken about, Aliskovic, who was also an active-duty policeman who caused the unfortunate incidents at the checkpoint that had been set up. Those were all active-duty policemen, not reserve policemen. Those were active-duty policemen. This was all done at the behest of Mr. Sarajlic because he was the most experienced, so to speak, among them. He only lived in Ljubija, but he worked in Prijedor. He was chief of a patrol of the traffic police, active-duty again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You referred to Mr. Aliskovic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: Yes. I know the man personally. I knew the other two also. Unfortunately, I couldn't bring myself to believe that all this would happen. They were all my friends from my former life in a manner of speaking, people I would see every day. Mr. Odobasic even played football with me. Part of his family lives in my house, so I just couldn't believe it. I've always been an optimist. I always believed that no such thing could ever happen. But everything that had gone on before, everything that I could see, pointed in that direction that these things would indeed happen. I was left alone believing that it couldn't happen, and those specific people, I just didn't think them capable of anything like that. I could give you a couple of other friends of mine that I stayed with until the very last minute, even the man who headed the attack on Prijedor, just two or three months before that, he was with me. I didn't go to Ljubija that often. He owned a cafe there. We spent time together in the cafe in the evening. We socialised, we played cards. The whole of the town knows it. This same man still lives in Ljubija, and it is public knowledge that he had taken part in an attack on Prijedor. I heard that there was a trial, that he was tried, but that he was released or set free. We are no longer in a position to socialise, but he still sees members of my family, father, mother, brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: Mr. Kanal Alagic -- Mr. Kemal Alagic who headed a group of people. He went to -- Ljubija is a mining village, and it's a mountain village. He went to a forest, the Kurevo forest. I suppose they were training people up there. They were organising this group of theirs. But again, I couldn't bring myself to believe that this would happen until the attack actually took place. But then all the worst suspicions were proven true up there in some operations carried out by the police and the army. Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 12113 to 12121. I knew friends from the police, friends of mine from the police who were killed there. Milan Cuk and I think another seven or eight young men belonging to Mr. Alagic's group.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In addition to working in an enterprise owned by Mr. Dragan Popovic, did you also during the war own your own petrol station?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: For a period of time, as I said, once we had managed to save the factory, I had an agreement with another company Dakomerc [phoen] where I came to work as a partner. We rented a petrol station, and we kept that petrol station for five years.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your petrol station, could one obtain petrol in return for vouchers?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: No, it was strictly privately owned, the petrol station. And as I've said before, I was not in favour of any such deals. I was not in favour of giving people petrol in exchange for certificates or vouchers. We only did favours occasionally to the medical centre when there was something urgent, when there was an urgency. We always had petrol. We had oil derivatives. I was in charge of procuring those. Everything was done by the book. Sometimes people would get fuel, but they had no money to pay. But this didn't happen very often. It was always for money, people were paying money. We didn't resell anything. Those were prices fixed by the state, and I'm sure that the police have their own records about all of these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there a petrol station in the town of Prijedor where you could obtain petrol in exchange for vouchers?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: Yes, that was the Energopetrol petrol station on the Banjacka Road where vouchers could be used to obtain petrol. It was a state-owned petrol station. That was the only place -- that was a place as far as I know where you could get petrol for vouchers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just for the sake of clarifying the transcript, can you please tell us again where this petrol station was, the Energopetrol petrol station.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: It was on the Prijedor/Banja Luka Road about 150 metres before you turn off to head for the town itself. It was on the Banja Luka/Novi Grad or Banja Luka/Prijedor Road around 100 metres from the junction where you turn off to head for the town itself. A hundred or a hundred fifty perhaps. This was an Energopetrol petrol station.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know where these vouchers were obtained in exchange for which certain organisations could obtain petrol at these petrol stations?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: As I said, for a while, I lived in Prijedor. I heard that there was a Crisis Staff and that they were distributing vouchers for petrol, for flour. I don't know about cigarettes, but I know that this Crisis Staff was distributing vouchers. I never used any of those myself. I didn't need any. Neither for myself nor for my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us where this Crisis Staff was based?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
