utterances.text: Yes, that was near where I lived. It was a Slovene company which held the premises prior to this newly-arisen situation. They were storing forest produce and fruits like mushrooms and forest fruits. I think the manager of the company was Boro -- I can't remember the last name. But I know the man's first name was Boro. I used to know him. It was a Slovene company. And that's the building, the premises, where the Crisis Staff was based.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what sort of a Crisis Staff that was and who sat on this Crisis Staff? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: Well, yeah. People would go there for flour, sugar, cigarettes, petrol vouchers. There were always people milling around there. I would often see Mr. Slobodan Kuruzovic there. I think he was the head of that Crisis Staff. Now, what else they were doing, I don't know. I just know that for these vouchers and for flour and cigarettes, you had to go there to get them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would the usher be so kind and show the witness the Exhibit Number S180, please. It's on page 38, item number 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Item number 22, I know you've probably never seen this document before, but I would like to ask you the following. And I can read, and then if you would please just follow. "At its meeting of the 5th of June, 1992, Prijedor municipal Crisis Staff pursuant to Article 7 of the decision on the organisation and work of Prijedor municipal Crisis Staff issued the following order: "The Serbian Territorial Defence Crisis Staff of Prijedor Municipality, which was dissolved by virtue of conclusion number 02-111-110/92 dated 29th of May, 1992, reached by Prijedor municipal Crisis Staff is hereby prohibited from issuing fuel receipts. All unused fuel receipts and the stamp are to be returned immediately to Prijedor Municipal Crisis Staff." This Crisis Staff that you were talking about, is it the same Crisis Staff the Serbian Territorial Defence Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: I don't know, but I can tell you something else. In all these -- most of these institutions, companies, and enterprises, all communities had some Crisis Staffs. As far as I know, this referred to -- I'm talking about Crisis Staffs across companies. For example, in Ljubija, we kept watch over the dam. There were guards, organised guards watching the dam. Over there, we had an artificial pond belonging to the iron ore mines. And there was a lot of quicksand there, and if the dam had burst, about 15 villages would have been wiped off the face of the earth. So I think that's more or less what you asked me about. I know that there was a Crisis Staff because I lived nearby. I know that people came there for petrol vouchers and that they could get petrol from the Energopetrol station. I know that people went there to obtain cigarettes and other provisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. As an employee of Mr. Popovic's company and as the owner of a petrol station, did you -- were you in possession of a permit to move about freely?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: I was not the owner. We were only leasing the petrol station. And now I'll answer the other question. Yes, I was in possession of such permit to move about. I obtained the permit personally from the SUP, the Secretariat of the Interior, from Mr. Simo Drljaca. It was from him that I obtained the permits to move about freely and to leave the country since I travelled abroad a lot to get oil derivatives. So I would usually be away for two or three days, and then I would be back at different intervals of time, 2.00 in the morning, 1.00 in the afternoon, constantly. So I was convinced that I needed to be in possession of a permit. I requested one, and I got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you in possession of a permit to move about during the curfew?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: Yes. As I said before, I did. The curfew in Prijedor was introduced at a certain point in time, and that was later. I can't remember exactly. I may be wrong as far as the date's concerned. But I think that was after the attack below Hambarine. Mr. Aliskovic and his group. A curfew was introduced between 10.00 in the evening -- from 10.00 in the evening to 6.00 in the morning. And yes, I did have the permit you asked me about. This permit was also issued by the SUP, the secretariat of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you were not mobilised during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: No, no, I wasn't mobilised. I had a work obligation assigned not only to me, but to other people, to all the working people, all working people had a work obligation. But I'm not sure that all those who had a work obligation were given a permit to move about freely during curfew. But I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say you obtained your permit to move about freely from Mr. Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Drljaca and how well?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: I did know him, but not well. I knew him just as well as I needed to know him. I know that he was the chief of the police centre. I know that he made the decisions, so I didn't need to go any further than that because it wouldn't have worked. I spoke to him, and I got what I had asked for. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it easy to work with Mr. Drljaca? Will you please describe for us the kind of personality, the kind of person that he was.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: Let me tell you one thing under those difficult circumstances, especially for me: I was a working person. It was hard to ask anyone for anything, let alone those special permits to move about freely. I didn't know what such a thing could have led other people to think or to believe. The times were hard, and Mr. Drljaca, at least that's what believed he was like, he was uncontested. He wouldn't ask anyone else. He was in charge of calling the shots. And if I had spoken to any of the other services, I would have gotten nowhere. He dealt with these things personally, and I got my permit from him. But he wasn't really very fond of doing things by the book or according to protocol. He made himself solely responsible for calling the shots. For example, if I had known someone who was close to him, probably I couldn't have obtained the permit in any other way except talking to him, going to talk to him myself. And I did believe that I did need those permits.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you in the town of Prijedor when the town was attacked on the 30th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: Yes. I was in possession of a permit, and I was not mobilised, as I've said. And people were talking, you know, you see one of my relatives was mobilised and this man is walking around quite free to do what he likes. So the times were hard and people could be suspicious or envious. But yes, I was in town the whole time. The petrol station -- the occasional pub or cafe, I lived alone unfortunately, so I took my meals in restaurants. Sometimes I would go and see my mother and father, so I was there. Unfortunately I was sleeping when the first attack started, but then immediately I woke up and one hour later I was standing outside. Movement was limited, but I was in possession of a permit that entitled me to move about anywhere, issued legally to me by the MUP. I went to all those places later on. I had a friend also, he is alive, but unfortunately he has now a severe handicap. Mr. Goran Dragojevic, who was an ambulance driver, he was headed out to give assistance to some people who had been wounded, but then he was mowed down under the fly-over there on his way to the SUP and the Ministry of the Interior. I think it was on the 20th early. I don't think he will ever fully recover from that. It's impossible. The wounds were too serious. But I know, as I say, I had another friend, I went around the whole place. There was fire burning near the Municipal Assembly building in the park where the museum was. That was the biggest fire. I'm not talking about the Stari Grad right now. I'm talking about the attack on the MUP building and the Municipal Assembly building. There was a museum there. Unfortunately, a lot of ammunition was found there, too, that had probably been brought there before. So the whole thing had been in preparation for at least several days. But again, as I say, I could never bring myself to believe it. If anyone had told me, I wouldn't have believed them. I know that in the Mladost sports hall, the leaders saw to it that people would be put up there, fed, and given room to sleep, a roof over their head, women and children, too. I know that some of the people who had at that point stayed at the Mladost hall later took part on the attack in Prijedor. I have just referred to a man who went from Ljubija who led a group from Ljubija consisting of between two and three hundred people. That's the estimate of how many there were. I know two or three people from that group. I know Kemal Alagic, their commander, personally. In Prijedor, I know a man who was a private entrepreneur like myself.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to repeat the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please just repeat the name of the person.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: Slavko Ecimovic. Slavko Ecimovic, Kemal Alagic, these were people who led the attack on our town. There were casualties. And the Stari Grad, the old town, a place of historical importance with old buildings, was set fire to and razed to the ground. They crossed the River Sana, and that's where the fighting took place, and near the museum, too, there was fighting -- or rather, from the museum in the direction of the MUP building and the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After these events, what was the situation like in Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: Let me tell you: Ljubija is a town for itself and there are a lot of things going on in Ljubija. I went there to see what my parents were doing, and there are Muslims, there are Croats, there are Serbs living together. And they asked me what was going on in Prijedor as if I had come from a different state. In Ljubija, everything was closer. Not many shops or bars in Ljubija, but whatever there were they were open. One could not feel in Ljubija any tensions. The situation was normal, so to speak. I came across a few Croats, a few Muslims. My house is very close to a -- the house of a Muslim family who are my acquaintances. I often visited them. Like I've already said, my Ljubija -- my town Ljubija is very closely connected with the mine, and the people had enjoyed support from each other. It was a mixed population. It was impossible that things were organised in Kurevo, and an attack would be launched from Kurevo, for those people to be fed up there and had arms there. It was impossible that all -- such things were organised by one person. After all the operations had taken place, it turned out that Mr. Alagic had been chased by police for five or six months, and he had his allies up there. So Mr. Alagic was not alone. There were other people with him up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In Ljubija, is the population still mixed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: Yes, the population is still mixed to this very day, although there's not much joy. There are a lot of refugees in Ljubija, but still people visit each other. There are a lot of returnees as well, people who have returned. And a lot of people had remained in Ljubija. Some people did leave, but a lot of them have returned. And I can say that Ljubija is again Ljubija as it used to be. As far as the composition of the population, people are still the same. None of the houses have been burned down. People who have returned were able to return to their own homes, and I don't think that anybody in Ljubija had any problems. There was no terrorism, there were no problems in Ljubija. I can give you the example of a place which is ethnically Croatian. And in that area, there were never either Serbs or Muslims. That's the village called Gornja Ravska. Nobody ever touched these people. Why? Because they never attacked anybody; they never touched anybody themselves. Children went to school. I can't say that people worked when all these things started because the mine had been closed, but they did stand guard in their respective companies, and they were involved in the protection of their own property. That's what they did. I know that they also participated in the mobilisation, that they responded to mobilisation calls which were sent to them as to everybody else. Those were mobilisation calls sent by the Territorial Defence. They didn't go to war because at that time there was no war. And these people still live there. They work in companies. They work on their farms. Those people are still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that some people have returned. When did people mostly leave Ljubija, in 1992 or 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: In 1995. Some people left in 1992, but those who left in 1992, they had some place to go, somewhere where they were better off than they would have been in Ljubija where there were some problems. But mostly people left in convoys in 1995. They went abroad. I can give you an example. One case that happened in October or November 1992. A family that I knew very well, the Causevic, Dzevad's family who -- he himself worked in the electrical company for ten years. He called me one day in 1992. I got into my car and went to his house. He said that he was afraid. He said: "My children are young. I have a brother in Slovakia. I would like to go and live with them." I told him: "Don't go. There's no need for you to go. My family is also here. My mother and father still live in Gornja Ljubija." Still he decided to leave. I couldn't persuade him to stay. On the following day, I again came in my car, and I drove him and his wife and his two children in my car to Prijedor. They spent the night in my place in Prijedor. And on the following day again I took all of them to joined the convoy that left via Novska. So they went abroad and eventually I believe they took residence in the Netherlands. His father and his mother had remained living there. People have returned, those who had stayed on, nothing happened to them. Nobody had anything bad happen to them if they didn't participate in war operations. Those people who manned the checkpoints, who were there, nobody touched them. And their houses also were not burnt down. I don't know whether they were plundered or not. I can't say anything about that. I didn't see anything like that personally. But I know that all the houses remained standing. None of them was burned down.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time, in spring and summer of 1992, did you hear of the existence of a body called the Crisis Staff of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know who its members were?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: I knew some of its members. Some people whom I met when I applied for my business programme. That's when I met Mr. Stakic. I also knew Ranko Travar who was a member of the Crisis Staff. Before that, he was the head of sales in Zito Promet. I also knew Mr. Slavko Budimir who was a teacher in the school in Cela. I went to that school for a year myself while the school in Prijedor was being refurbished. That's how I met Mr. Slavko Budimir. I met him in 1976. I also knew Ranko Travar from 1986 or 1987. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In the past, the Defence always corrected the transcript when Prosecution counsel spoke about Crisis Staff of the Municipal Assembly. And it was your submission that it was on purpose to confuse the words "Municipal Assembly" and "municipal." I think the word correct on page 60, line 5, in your question should be "the Prijedor municipal Crisis Staff." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prastalo, did you personally attend any of the meetings of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: No, I never attended a meeting of the Crisis Staff. I don't know why I should be. I was not a member of any party ever. Why would I then attend a meeting of the Crisis Staff? I was not interested in that. I was not interested in its work, what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time, did you socialise with some of the members of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: Yes. I would see Slavko from time to time. I would also see Mr. Travar from time to time. I would see Dr. Stakic as well. As I say, Dr. Stakic received us in his office to discuss the company that we were trying to incept. That's how I met him. I immediately liked him as a person. He was fighting for the things for which I'm fighting to this day. He wanted things to be privatised. He wanted people to be paid according to their work. He didn't want anybody to work for free. He wanted the work of an individual to be valued. And that's what I liked about Dr. Stakic. That's when I met him, and after that we socialised quite often. And this was mostly to do with sports. We would talk about football. I was quite familiar with things that were taking place in football. Sometimes we would even play together. We would also exchange opinions on business, on work, when we had time. I think - I don't know for sure - but I think that Dr. Stakic found himself in that place by mistake. I don't think that this position is influential. Nobody sitting in that position had any real say because if he had had a real say, he would have done something for me. He would have given me a permit to move about. He would have given me a permit to leave the country. He would have given me a building plot where to build my factory. But he couldn't do that. But he still fought for things. We were talking about the oil for -- that was needed for the sowing. We were talking about whether that oil could be obtained or not, things like that. The two of us, we fought for the same things, and we were also rivals in sports. We would play football together if we had time, whenever we had time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Did you play football together or something else?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: No, we played pools, but we talked about football because I spent a lot -- a number of years playing football, and we talked about football and we played billiards together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please be so kind and concentrate your questions on the time relevant under the fourth amended indictment or, if you want to touch on other time frames, please ask the witness what he is discussing right now. From the last two pages, it does not transpire when this was, when you socialised with Dr. Stakic, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will ask you, according to His Honour Schomburg's instructions, when you socialised with Dr. Stakic, did that take place when Dr. Stakic was a member of the Crisis Staff, that is, in spring and summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I met Dr. Stakic when he received us in his office to discuss the building of our factory and the purchase of the land where we were going to build the factory. At that time, Dr. Stakic was the vice-president of the Municipal Assembly, and sometimes we would see each other socially. But we were -- we would play billiards. And that continued later on, a bit more intensively. There were a few of us private entrepreneurs who worked at the time who were members of the business community and the door to the Municipal Assembly building was always open to us. But whenever we came, we went to the Executive Board because it was the Executive Board who could do things for us and who could make decisions in our favour. It was not the president or the vice-president of the Municipal Assembly that could do that. When we had business to discuss with anybody, we had to discuss it with the Executive Board. When you asked me about the Crisis Staff, I believe that I've already told you that. I've already answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Dr. Stakic ever talk to you about the purchase of fuel for sowing and for harvest and how was that done?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: Yes. Since my business was also oil derivatives and at that time, there was no cash, and at one point Dr. Stakic told me that he would try and obtain fuel from the commodity reserves. And that that fuel would be used for sowing and for harvest. He asked me if I could help him and if we could do that without any commission or fee. This oil from commodity reserve was sold at 55 and 50 Phennigs a litre. One price was for sowing and the other was for harvesting. He put that proposal forward before the Executive Board. The Executive Board approved that. We obtained the derivatives from the commodity reserves. Then we distributed that oil at some places where it was very difficult for the population to obtain it. We transported that oil by our own system. We did not consider that a lucrative business, but we thought it was a good thing to do. We did that one year for the sowing and harvest season. And this was all thanks to Dr. Stakic who asked us to do that and who organised everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the witness, was this before the 6th of June, 1992, or after the 6th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The oil was purchased before the 6th of June, a certainty quantity. That was for the harvest of that year. Some oil was obtained in winter and some in spring. There were two rounds of distribution. There may have been a delay in the distribution, but that delay was only for about 10 or 15 days. So there were two distribution rounds for the oil that was distributed for the harvest and sowing seasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So the first round of distribution would be before the 30th of April, 1992, or after the 30th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the 30th of April, there was a distribution of derivatives, and there was a certain schedule. First, we would go to the Executive Board. The Executive Board would allocate oil by the local communes, and the local communes apply for the oil based on the acreage of land. So the quantity of oil depended on the acreage of land. The second distribution was for the sowing season which was sometime in June of that year. In that area, sowing usually takes place in July. So we obtained fuel both for the sowing period and for the harvest period. The secretaries of the local communes were supposed to go to the Executive Board with their lists of requirements, and then the Executive Board would allocate vouchers for the oil in different local communes based on the list of their requirements which were submitted to them by the secretaries of the communes. The oil was then obtained by Serbs, Croats, Muslims. Everybody who had proof that they had arable land were in the position to obtain that fuel from the commodity reserves at my petrol station. For the period of five years that I leased that petrol station, everybody could obtain oil from my petrol station regardless of their ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask a third time, you mentioned on page 33, today's LiveNote, line 20, "he - it is Dr. Stakic - put that proposal forward before the Executive Board. The Executive Board approved that." When was it in 1992? As precise as possible. I know it's difficult ten years ago, more than ten years ago.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992, that was -- are you asking me to give you the exact date? I'm afraid I can't remember the exact date. It was sometime in April. I can't remember the exact date. I don't remember whether it was the end of April or the beginning of May. I said a little while ago that there was a slight delay in the purchase of the derivative in that first round. There was a slight delay, so I don't know whether it was in the -- in late April or the beginning of May. But I don't think it's important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May it assist you. I asked you for a concrete point in time you mentioned in your own testimony, and it's for us to find out when this point was exactly in time. So was it in a period of time Dr. Stakic was still the vice-president or was he already the president of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was the president. So that was -- I believe that was before the 5th of May or the 6th of May. Because the first quantity of fuel -- this was the first intervention on the part of the Municipal Assembly that was in favour of the agricultural sector. So the delivery of these derivatives and the distribution that was for the sowing was almost at the time when there was already the harvest period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I believe that the confusion arose from the following: Is the company owned by Mr. Popovic and the petrol station that you leased, are these two different things? Maybe that is the source of the confusion.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: Yes, these are two different things.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you applied for a permit to purchase the land to build the factory owned by Mr. Popovic, what was Dr. Stakic at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic at that time was the vice-president when we applied for a permit to build the factory, because we built that factory in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you applied for the fuel, that is, when it was asked from you to help with the distribution of fuel for sowing, what was Mr. Stakic at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: The president of the municipality. We talked about all that even before, and I didn't know on that same day what would happen. We were talking about fuel, about oil. We discussed general business matters. So when I said that for the first time there was an intervention, I'm talking about the delivery of oil both for sowing and for other harvest. And this was distributed across the board to the entire population, to Muslims, Croats, and Serbs alike, whoever could obtain fuel was able to obtain it. They came with pieces of papers stamped by the Executive Board and by their respective local commune, and they would arrive at the petrol station with buckets and what have you to obtain the petrol that they were entitled to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The first round of distribution of fuel for the sowing, according to you, may have been towards the beginning of May?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We spoke about you socialising with Dr. Stakic. You discussed football. You played pool.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: Only when we had time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you spoke about business, whenever you discussed business, did Mr. Stakic ever tell you about the activities of the Crisis Staff or what it did?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: No, not really. I told you what we talked about. I should be able to assume what the activities of the Crisis Staff might be, general needs of the population, the economy, communal infrastructure. We had problems with the water lines, with different kinds of cisterns. I told you already what the Crisis Staff was doing when I lived over there. I think it was like a central office, a headquarters, where the different Crisis Staffs from the local communes and different companies were organised. I think the Crisis Staff, the Crisis Staff made such decisions as far as I believe. We never -- we always tried to as much as we could, like I said, to stick to our business. I had my own things to follow, and the doctor had his own business. We often discussed private initiative in business. The doctor wanted to have a private surgery, so we talked along those lines. But that was really all we ever discussed. We never discussed politics, and I was myself never a member of any party.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Talking about party membership, I would like to ask you something about the events following September 1992. You spoke about this group - we shall not name them now - the group who tried to take away from you the enterprise which you now ran. Do you know anything about the attempts to remove Dr. Stakic from the autumn of 1992 onwards?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: Yes, I do know about that. That group, and I think I am well-placed to know it, because that was more my concern than his, that was the opposition who had told me even before they came to power that they would take my factory away from me. They tried, but they failed. They had Dr. Stakic removed. I think the chief of the SUP was also removed at that time. People from the municipality were removed, and they appointed their own people. Should I say who held the different positions? Should I give you the names? The names of the people who were subsequently appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As long as you don't have a problem with that, please do.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: No, I don't. Quite the contrary. Dr. Stakic was replaced and Mr. Kurnoga was appointed. In what way -- exactly what the procedure was - whether there was a municipal decision or whether this was voted on - but I know that Kurnoga became the president of the assembly. I know that Dr. Stakic was mobilised after he had been removed to the army probably. I was never mobilised myself, and I was quite surprised not to be. That was something out of the ordinary. I suppose Dr. Stakic was not much to their liking because I find I have to repeat this for the umpteenth time, he was a person who was more into business actually all the way, whereas the more radical group, the radical group had no understanding for this. They denied everything. And I think it's quite obvious what they did and what they were good for. I think they are going to be remembered for that. Money ran out. Companies went bankrupt or were ruined. No care was taken of them. People's companies and pubs were taken from them. It had never before been common practice where we used to live taking other people's things. I never did this myself in my whole life. I never asked anyone for anything. Again, I must say this radical group arrived, and as far as I know, Dr. Stakic was subsequently mobilised to the Republika Srpska army. How he was mobilised or who he mobilised by, I really don't know. His successors obviously didn't like him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like to mention page 69, line 8, it says "whereas the more radical group," and the witness says "the radical group." And in this sentence, we have both, but "more radical group" has never been mentioned. So if you want, I can clarify it with the witness, or it can be checked through the audiotape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I would ask you to repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You heard what my intervention was about.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I said the radical group. The people who had been in power before them, I think, were moderate. Those people who had been before them tried to deal with the economy, to do something about it. And the new people who replaced them were radical people. They wanted power at all cost. So I told you about my problem with them in the opposition, and then they tried to carry this out once they came to power. But this was not only about myself. I think there must have been other such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said you had talked to them even before they had Dr. Stakic removed. When they were removing him, did they refer to his membership in any of the political parties?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: Well, as I told you, I was socialising with different people. So very often, we would sit together. Sometimes the conversation was pleasant, about pleasant subjects, and sometimes we would clash verbally. But when we talked, they said "how can someone be the president of the Municipal Assembly and not even a member of the SDS"? I heard this. I heard people say this. I didn't know, but I heard that he was not a member of the SDS, Dr. Stakic. I heard that he had earlier been a member of the People's Radical Party Nikola Pasic. I don't know if they were saying that he couldn't be the president of the assembly if he wasn't a member of the SDS, but I didn't understand that. But that's how it goes over there. We must be in power. We are the SDS members. And those were the strongmen, the radical group within the SDS, the people I've already named.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You told us when you first met Dr. Stakic and how often and when you socialised with him. Did you ever hear him give a speech on the radio or did you read any of his speeches in the papers or any of his public addresses?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: In our municipality, we have the Kozarski Vjesnik newspaper. Dr. Stakic once, when there was a formal or a ceremonial occasion when a factory was being opened or a production floor or maybe there was some humanitarian action, so holding the position that he was holding at the time, of course, he appeared as a representative of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you socialise with Dr. Stakic also in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: Yes, not right away, due to the nature of my job. I travel very often, I travel abroad. I travel all over Yugoslavia. But I found out that Dr. Stakic was specialising medicine in Belgrade. I can't remember the name of the hospital, but it is in the part of town called Banjica. It's something to do with the bones. I can't remember the name. I did go looking for him once, and I found him there. So we started socialising there in Belgrade. Whenever we had some spare time, maybe once, two, three times a month depending on the extent of our professional activities, sometimes we would see each other four or five time a months, sometimes once a month depending. Lately, we have been spending more time together. Dr. Stakic's family are all very pleasant people, and he was a family man. He really loved his family. We all love our family, of course. But if I look at myself, I never had enough time to go and speak to my children's teachers at school, to help them do their homework, or anything like that. Dr. Stakic, on the other hand, always made time to do this, and he always did this as far as I know in his family life. His family always came first, and then friends. I can't say we came second, but we were there. He cared about us. He had a normal life. He was specialising in his branch of medicine. I think he specialised in two different areas actually. We went out together in Belgrade whenever we had time. We would go to a pub for a drink. We would go to a football match, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only one further question: You said you were in possession of a permit to move about freely during curfew.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To move about freely during curfew.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you told Dr. Stakic about this, what was his reaction?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO
utterances.text: He smiled. I couldn't believe, but I do believe it now when he told me that he didn't have a permit even when he was working in the Crisis Staff. But he said he was not in possession of a permit. The only people who had these permits were people who were pursuing some activity, who were into business. Simo Drljaca issued these. And the SUP only issued these for moving about freely during curfew and for leaving the country. So probably Dr. Stakic never qualified to have one like that issued to him because he wasn't friends maybe with some of those people who were in charge of issuing those permits. That's my understanding at least. But these permits were used to enable one to move about freely around the clock in the town of Prijedor, and they were issued by the MUP. But as far as I heard, none of the members of the Crisis Staff were actually in possession of such permits, and I think altogether perhaps 15 people had such permits. That's we they don't include the professional police units who were free to move about. The whole thing didn't last for too long. Curfew was introduced when the killings in Hambarine took place at the checkpoint set up by Aliskovic. Aside from that, in the town up to that point, you had been able to move about freely and everyone did. Shops were open. There were two open-air markets. Everyone was normal, the hospital. Everyone was business as usual prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Prastalo. For the time being I have no further questions to ask you. Now you'll have asked a number of questions by my learned friend and colleague from the Prosecution and after that by the Honourable Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just to stay in context of family life, may I ask you, when you met Dr. Stakic in Belgrade, did you meet also the family of Dr. Stakic in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That day, when I went looking for Dr. Stakic, I didn't meet his family on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not his family was in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if they were there at that time. I found Dr. Stakic. I spent some time with him at the hospital where he was, an hour perhaps. That's as long as he could afford. I didn't go anywhere with Dr. Stakic at that time except the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. It was just for clarification because it was in that context. For procedural reasons, unfortunately we can't continue from the side of the Bench with the cross-examination today. May I ask the Prosecution, Prosecution would be prepared to continue with the cross-examination already tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then you are excused for today. And I have to ask you to come back tomorrow, 9.00, same courtroom. And please, as it is the rule, don't contact one of the parties, Prosecution or Defence, during your stay, and please don't contact other witnesses you may meet here in The Hague, and especially don't discuss issues of your testimony. Thank you for today. And may I ask the usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before the break, that the parties know what we have to discuss, it's a question of the admission or the possibility -- at least the possibility of admission into evidence of witnesses under 92 bis. We will after deliberations proceed in the following order: That we first revisit the final witness list updated as of today in order to find out whether or whether not a witness on this list can be admitted under Rule 92 bis and whether or whether not the one or other witness in the light of that what we have already heard and which seems to be proven can be deleted from the original witness list. Then following this, we would turn to defendant Milomir Stakic's motion for leave to introduce written statements pursuant to Rule 92 bis. I don't want to comment this motion that has nothing to do with our rules in this moment. No doubt that the first step has to be, following our rules, 73 ter(D), that the Defence would have, if it considers it to be in the interests of justice, file a motion to reinstate the list of witnesses or to vary the decision as to which witnesses are to be called. You are requesting additional witnesses, and this is the first step to decide whether or not we add witnesses to the final -- provisional final list of witnesses following Rule 73 ter(C). The second step will then be, and this is the question before us, whether or whether not to grant in principle that it might be a statement under 92 bis. But at the same time, I invite the Prosecution to indicate already now that it might be or it might not be that the one or other witness is precluded from the outset or excluded from the outset under Rule 92 bis because it doesn't meet the prerequisites laid down in Rule 92 bis(A). And only then we can decide what has to follow. The final decision whether or not a statement under Rule 92 bis is admissible can only be made when we have this statement. And it's only then for the Prosecution to decide whether or not they request cross-examination and, as indicated in our decision, it is finally for the Trial Chamber to decide whether or not in the light of the then statement we want to hear the witness as a live witness. Before I forget the additional items, I want to ask, (a), the audio unit to check again page 69, line 5 to 9, and to print out what has been said by the witness of today. Then we have before us the question of the -- how to take the videoconference. I'm extremely grateful that the registry on her own initiative made the necessary preparations for interpretation being present in -- I think it will be in Banja Luka for next week. Therefore, the interpretation will be provided by CLSS staff for 92 bis statements. As regards the videolink -- sorry, as regards now the videolink, the rule will be that it will be as it was during the Prosecution videolink in the Prosecution case, that the witness is not allowed to have any kind of statement in front of the witness. And in addition, there should be no other person, no representative of one of the parties present in the same room when the witnesses will be heard during the videolink. The videolink will cause some problems on Thursday as to the fact that we have to conclude the hearings on Thursday a quarter to 5.00 because as of 5.00 next Thursday, the election of the new president of this Tribunal will take place. I hope, but this is only a hope, that the video hearings nevertheless can be concluded during the next week, and I already asked the registry to find out whether or not it will be possible to have an additional time frame or window where these video testimonies can be given in and from Banja Luka. So far for the moment, we will start this exercise going through once again the witness list immediately after the break. The trial stays adjourned until 3.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. The point of departure is no doubt the scheduling order from the 12th of February, 2003. And the Trial Chamber's decision dated also the 12th of December. Let us please first try that we can arrange the necessary especially after the itineraries that we can find out whether or whether not the one or the other witness being on the so-called final witness list can be for the reasons given deleted or this witness can be 92 bissed. So we already indicated in our order what are the persons still on the witness list and not yet heard who in any event from the perspective of the Bench has to be heard as live witnesses. So then let us start -- I think the order would be appropriate first for the Defence to give some comments whether they need, in fact, the witness, and then immediately the answer whether this would be appropriate under 92 bis, and the basis that what we call the provisional proffers we received from the Defence. We would start with witness number 1, Aleksic Rade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we think that he is an important witness because he works for the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps -- I just want to caution everyone that we're in open session. I don't know if we mention any names that the Defence has not checked on in protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then let's mention the 65 ter numbers, 001. I understand your contribution. What about Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We think this witness should be live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: That's what we said. Then 004.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This witness is scheduled to be testifying through the videolink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And may I ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He's a non-Serb living in Prijedor in that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The question is only relating to the itinerary. It's only related to 92 bis witnesses that some should be heard in Banja Luka, others in Belgrade. And the videolink would be only from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Only to be absolutely sure. Then 006.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This witness is scheduled as a live witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And may we ask, as ordered, what would be the correct name? Do we need to go into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For this witness, yes, I think that he would be asking for protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then, please, private session.
